author: Cas Smith
title: Anti-war activists prepare to protest Land Forces weapons expo
content:
As the third anniversary of Israel’s assault on Gaza nears a coalition of anti-war activists is preparing to protest against the Land Forces International Land Defence Exposition. 

Cas Smith

 reports.

author: Alex Salmon
title: The absent history of social upheaval after WWI
content:
Riots: Returned soldiers and public disorder in Australia at the end of World War I By Fiona Skyring Perth: UWA Press November, 2025 225pp RRP $39.99

Peace Day celebrations were held across Australia on November 14, 1918, following the end of World War I.

Even though the shooting had barely ended, the social tensions created by the war would be exposed in riots and brawls involving returned soldiers in Adelaide, Broken Hill and Townsville. These were predecessors to the riots that occurred from 1919–21.

Author and historian Fiona Skyring explores this history in her 2025 book, Riots: Returned soldiers and public disorder in Australia at the end of World War I.

In Townsville and Broken-Hill, riots and brawls occurred between self-styled “loyalist” soldiers and trade unionists, socialists and anti-conscriptionists. In Adelaide, soldiers showed their support to striking tram drivers, 300 of whom had served in the Australian Imperial Forces (AIF), by organising and attacking strikebreakers.

The Australia that WWI soldiers returned to was deeply divided by class, religion, social and political issues. The country had been rocked by the 1916–17 anti-conscription referenda, the 1917 New South Wales general strike, and international events such as 1916 Irish Easter Uprising, the 1917 Russian Revolution and the 1918–19 influenza pandemic.

In 1918–19 these divisions continued, as t

author: Markela Panegyres
title: Macklemore strikes a blow for the cultural intifada
content:
When United States rap artist Macklemore was dropped from pop singer Ed Sheeran’s US tour for saying “Free Palestine” during a concert, it sparked a global wave of support for Macklemore, and widespread condemnation of Sheeran’s refusal to take a stand on Palestine.

Billionaire Zionist Robert Kraft, owner of the Gillette Stadium where Macklemore was scheduled to perform, claimed the rapper had performed “hate speech” and pushed for his removal. The Israeli-American Council (IAC) petitioned against Macklemore, and pop singer PINK amplified social media posts by the Zionist StopAntisemitism group, claiming Macklemore had “accused Israel of a false ‘genocide’”, and “turned a mainstream event into a political nightmare against the Jewish state”.

Sheeran subsequently released a weak public response, playing down the genocide as a “conflict” and claiming he was trying to use his platform as a “sanctuary” outside politics. But as the Palestinian Campaign for the Academic and Cultural Boycott of Israel (PACBI) pointed out, Sheeran’s statement “both-sides Israel’s ongoing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza” and repeats “anti-Palestinian Israel lobby talking points that deny the genocide and want to whitewash apartheid”.

The attempt to silence Macklemore galvanised Palestinian and non-Palestinian artists and their supporters. It also brought to the fore the words of Paul Robeson, d

author: Jim McIlroy
title: Baird forced to resign over bid to privatise Big Bash League
content:
Former NSW Liberal Premier Mike Baird has resigned as chair of Cricket Australia (CA) as opposition grows to its proposed privatisation of the Big Bash League (BBL) — the Australian 20 over competition.

Former Australian Test batsman David Boon will take over as CA interim chair.

Baird has long been a privatisation crusader, particularly as NSW premier over 2014-2017, when he privatised and sold off the state-owned power facility Ausgrid and pushed to privatise huge swathes of public land, buildings and other assets.

He also rammed through major parts of the federal Coalition’s public sector cuts.

It should therefore come as no surprise that he played a key role in CA’s campaign to sell off major parts of the BBL to private investors.

Baird was told mid September that Cricket NSW, chaired by John Knox, had withdrawn support for him to take another three-year term. It also rejected a suggestion that Baird move into a recently-vacated independent director’s spot, until a new chair could be found.

Cricket NSW slammed CA’s decision to introduce private investment earlier this month. “This decision risks leaving cricket in NSW and Australia strategically and financially worse off, with direct consequences for our ability to invest in grassroots cricket,” it said on September 9.

author: Brian Mahony
title: Coffs Harbour council rescinds climate emergency declaration
content:
Coffs Harbour City Council voted 4–3 on September 24 to rescind its 2022 declaration of a climate emergency.

The motion was put by Mayor Nikki Williams, who also sought to remove Scope 3 emissions from the council’s Renewal Energy and Emissions Reduction Plan (REERP) and delay accepting the plan for several months.

Williams stood as an independent, but local media has reported that she is a member of the National Party.

Greens Councillor Jonathan Cassell, who put the initial climate emergency motion in 2022, said council had “smash[ed] climate action in our council for the foreseeable future”.

“Climate inaction is costing us more and more, and if we aren’t prepared to act swiftly and urgently to address climate change then we are going to pay more in future.”

The 2022 motion passed 5–4, after impassioned speeches from students from local high schools who called for urgent action on climate change.

author: Maharnav Bhuyan, Chloe DS
title: Labor singles out international students for attack
content:
Federal Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke announced on September 17 that most international students will no longer be able to bring their partners, or children, to Australia.

Burke told the National Press Club that the ban covers new student visa applicants and people applying for the Temporary Graduate visa, which allows students to work here after completing their studies. He said the new measures will protect the “integrity” of the visa system.

Labor’s family ban is the latest in a series of measures that make it harder and more expensive for international students to come to Australia and stay after their graduate.

The Senate rejected Labor’s attempt to cap international student numbers in 2024. It then introduced other measures to reduce student numbers, including slower visa processing and higher fees.

The student visa application fee was $710 in 2023, rising to $1600 in 2024, $2000 in 2025 and $2500 in July. Applicants lose the fee if their visa application is refused. They must also show that they have at least $29,710 for a year’s living costs, on top of tuition and travel costs.

The Temporary Graduate visa has also become more expensive. The application fee rose from $2300 at the start of the year to $4600 in March and $5750 in July.

The road to permanent residency is also narrowing. In 2024–25, 12,637 people moved from a student visa to permanent residency. Tha

author: Rachel Evans
title: Call for Hamas, Hezbollah to be de-listed from terrorism register
content:
An anti-war action at Newtown Station on September 26 called for Australia to remove pro-Palestine groups from the terrorism list. Australia has 31 organisations on its list of terrorist groups.

Speakers called on the Australian government to take Palestine-based group Hamas, Lebanon’s Hezbollah, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and others off the list of proscribed terrorist groups. They said Palestine is resisting a genocide and Australia needs to support those resisting.

They also called on Australia to demand Israel release paediatrician Dr Hussam Abu Safiya, whose life is in danger in an Israeli prison.

The right to independence movements to resist is recognised by a 1982 United Nations General Assembly resolution, where it states that resistance and armed struggle is a legitimate tactic of the struggle for “independence, territorial integrity, national unity and liberation from colonial domination, apartheid and foreign occupation”.

The action was organised by Sydney Palestine Action, Trotskyist Platform, Nurses and Midwives for Palestine, Weapons Out of the West and Pride In Protest.

author: Gandipan Nantha Gopalan, Peter Boyle
title: PSM: Does Malaysia’s data centre boom serve the people?
content:
Malaysia is experiencing an unprecedented Artificial Intelligence (AI) data centre boom, with AI data centres having overtaken manufacturing as the major destination for investment in the country.

Data centre and cloud computing projects, totalling RM95.8 billion (A$33.44 billion), accounted for almost 44% of Malaysia’s approved investments in the first half of last year. Since 2021, approved data centre investments have totalled RM385.7 billion (A$134.62 billion).

However, if the government wants Malaysians to celebrate this investment boom, it should publicly release the full balance sheet on jobs, economic development and environmental impacts, Socialist Party of Malaysia (PSM) deputy secretary-general Gandipan Nantha Gopalan, told Green Left’s Peter Boyle.

What are these data centres being used for and whose interests do they serve?

Data centres are the physical infrastructure behind much of the digital economy. They store and process data, run cloud services and increasingly provide the computing power needed for AI training and inference. The important questions that everyone should ask are who owns it, who controls it and who captures the economic value generated from it.

Malaysia has attracted major global operators and investors including AWS, Microsoft, Google, Bridge Data Centres, DayOne, AirTrunk and Vantage Data Centres. It is time, as a Global South country,

author: Ishita Chakrabarty
title: Hindus for Human Rights: ‘Racism is not just about violence, it manifests through misinformation’
content:
To all those who have come from far off-lands and continents; who have made it here despite the monumental barriers that passport privilege poses for some over others — the intense questioning as to motivation; the demand for return tickets; the visa costs that keep escalating year on year; the bank statements and medical reports to prove you will not become a burden onto the system, I am one among you.

To those who have lived here for generations and are yet still told to “Go back where you came from”.

To those who hold a sacred relationship to this land — whose belonging to this land can never be severed by the operation of an unjust, extractive and foreign imposed law.

And to all those who join us here in solidarity, who believe in the idea of an inclusive, egalitarian and multicultural Australia.

I come from Bengal in India. I am representing Hindus for Human Rights, a voice for progressive Hindus and Indians working for inter-faith and inter-community respect and understanding and advocating against all kinds of discrimination and bigotry.

Coming from India, I know all too well what hate, bigotry and the belief of the superiority of some over the other looks like, and how the destruction of the very fabric of society is tantamount to the destruction of the human within us.

It is because of the love I hold towards my home country and the appreciation for being here th

author: Mat Ward
title: 10 essential new protest albums everyone needs to hear
content:
Do you think there’s no good protest music these days? So did I, until I started looking for it. Every month, I listen to it all, then select the best that relates to that month’s political news. Here’s the round-up for September.

US rapper Macklemore called for a "free Palestine" from the stage while supporting pop megastar Ed Sheeran on September 4. His speech, along with his politically-themed set, sparked a petition from the Israeli American Council. Jewish billionaire Robert Kraft refused to let Macklemore play at a stadium he owns and rallied other stadium owners to do the same. Sheeran - who claims to be politically neutral despite supporting multiple leftist causes in the past - announced he was dropping Macklemore from the tour. As a result, all of Sheeran's support acts dropped out to protest against Macklemore's cancellation. On the same day Macklemore kicked off the controversy, US-Jordanian rapper Eddy Mack released his new album, which opens with the pro-Palestine song "Can't Cancel Me". Days later, he posted a photo of himself with Macklemore, who then announced his own "Free Palestine" tour. LISTEN>>>

author: Kerry Smith
title: No conviction recorded against anti-genocide Pine Gap activists
content:
The Alice Springs Magistrates Court decided on September 14 not to record a criminal conviction against two activists, charged with “failing to cease to loiter” on a public road near the United States spy base Pine Gap in the Northern Territory last October.

Jorgen Doyle and Yul Scarf locked on to 44-gallon drum, filled with concrete, on a public road on Arrente Country for nine hours to protest Australian complicity to the genocide in Gaza through intelligence provided by Pine Gap.

The action prevented Pine Gap workers from accessing the base. It was the third action Mparntwe for Falastin had organised.

Doyle and Scarf tendered evidence that their actions were motivated by their sincerely held beliefs — borne out by the facts — that Pine Gap is contributing intelligence to the Israeli military to facilitate its ongoing genocidal war.

Doyle said the action helped to highlight Pine Gap’s role in the genocide in Gaza. “Pine Gap is sharing surveillance data, including geolocation information from mobile phones, with the genocidal Israeli regime, who are targeting journalists and their families, children, teachers, doctors, patients and the entire population of Palestine”.

The court heard from expert witnesses Richard Tanter and Chris Sidoti.

Sidoti is a former senior member of the UN’s Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory. Tha

author: Arlo Valmai
title: Communities say ‘Unite against racism’
content:
A community speak-out and banner drop against racism in the inner city suburb of Glebe drew about 50 people on September 26 despite the unusual heat.

Carolyn Ienna, Wiradjuri person and Glebe-based artist and activist, gave the acknowledgment of Country and a statement from Uncle Raymond Minniecon, responding to Hanson’s comment that Aboriginal people are the “most primitive race” was read out.

Speakers included Ethan Floyd, USyd student and community organiser; Ishita Chakrabarty from Hindus for Human Rights; Divya from University of NSW SRC and Grassroots; Rachel Evans, Socialist Alliance candidate for Heffron; Theodore, a year-12 student who helped organise the walk-out against Pauline Hanson; and Isaac Nellist, Socialist Alliance candidate for Balmain.

They all called for united action to stop the rise of the far right and highlighted Labor and the Coalition’s complicity in normalising racism and divisive politics.

The rally marched down Glebe Point Road and along Parramatta Road to the University of Sydney footbridge where they held up giant lettering which read “UNITE AGAINST RACISM”. Drivers tooted in support.

Racists had used the same bridge, which crosses the bust Parramatta Road, to unfurl their hateful slogans several months back.

The community action was organised by Socialist Alliance and widely endorsed by community and activist groups.

author: Pip Hinman
title: Albanese’s United Nations climate hypocrisy
content:
Anthony Albanese’s speech to the United Nations during “climate week” revealed just how out of touch he and his government is with the widespread community concern over runaway climate change.

Albanese delivered a sort of homily in New York. He said scientists have “warned” us about climate change and that Australia “understands the dangers of global warming and the urgency of climate action”.

He went on to praise firefighters and special emergency service workers for showing the “best of humanity” in the 2019-20 Black Summer bushfire crises and various devastating floods.

With hand on heart, Albanese said: “There’s no avoiding the scale of our responsibility — or the cost of inaction”, before going on to praise Australians for “choosing to electrify” with “clean, reliable, more affordable energy”.

While rooftop solar energy powers at least 13% of our energy, and Australia is on track to meet its rooftop solar targets, it is a wrong to argue, as Albanese essentially did, that the climate can be “saved” by individual households choosing to go green.

As long as the big polluters — fossil fuel corporations — continue to be subsidised by govenrments, climate change will worsen. The Climate Council has done the research and said the big polluters are expected to reduce their share by just 7.6% over the five years to 2030, compared to a 19% reduction across the rest of the count

author: Isaac Nellist, Chiara Reeves
title: USyd students vote to cut ties with Israel
content:
Students at the University of Sydney (USyd) have overwhelmingly voted for an academic boycott of Israel in a referendum held alongside elections for the Student Representative Council (SRC) over September 22–24.

Honi Soit reported that more than 3500 students, 86% of the 4065 students who voted, were in favour of calling on USyd to adopt an “academic boycott policy against Israeli institutions complicit in apartheid and genocide”.

The referendum motion called on the university to cut ties with Israeli universities, including Tel Aviv University, Technion and the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.

It also called on management to “end all research partnerships with weapons companies supplying Israel” and for the SRC to “support the struggle for Palestinian freedom”.

All four candidates for SRC President supported the referendum, including incumbent president Grace Street from Grassroots, Emma Searle from Socialist Alternative (SAlt), Ava Cavalerie from National Labor Students (NLS) and Vieve Carnsew from Solidarity.

The referendum was activated by Carnsew and Students Against War/Solidarity after they collected at least 500 signatures.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese gave Carnsew and Solidarity’s “Globalise the Intifada” ticket more coverage by describing it as a “hateful slogan”.

Albanese, NSW Premier Chris Minns and federal Education Minister Jason Clare reportedly contacte

author: Renfrey Clarke
title: Whyalla Steel sackings show need for public ownership
content:
The firm of administrators charged with selling the Whyalla Steelworks plant in South Australia announced on September 14 that efforts to repair the plant’s blast furnace had been abandoned. Smelting of iron ore would cease and of the plant’s total of close to 1700 regular workers, some 500 would lose their jobs.

Joining them would be about 100 “labour hire” workers and many of the 200 “embedded contractors” working at the plant but employed by other companies.

It is hard to overstate the impact of the sackings on Whyalla and its 21,000 people. It is thought that about five further local jobs are to be created from the spending of each full-time steelworks employee. A huge chunk of money will thus be gouged out of the city’s narrowly-based economy. Small businesses will shut their doors, and property values will crash.

One of many ironies is that demand for the steel plant’s main products remains strong.

Whyalla, in recent years, has produced about three-quarters of Australia’s structural steel and all of the country’s output of “long products” such as steel rails and girders. Production of these goods will continue, with the plant’s rolling mill processing imports of semi-finished steel “blooms”. Also carrying on will be production — now for shipment elsewhere — of smelter-ready iron ore pellets, on the basis of the ore resources of the nearby Middleback Range.

author: Beau Lyons
title: Snap action calls for suspended teacher to be reinstated
content:
NSW Activist Teachers Network organised a snap rally outside the Department of Education on September 24 for John Morris, a teacher who was suspended without pay after a dishonest smear campaign from the Daily Telegraph for posting about Palestine on his own social media page.

Speakers included Cassandra Barford, Nurses and Midwives for Palestine, Nick Reimer, Vice President (academic) of the Sydney University National Tertiary Education branch, Yehuda Aaron, a Jewish teacher and member of Teachers and School Staff for Palestine and Alex McKinnon, from Deep Cut News.

People were urged to join the campaign to boycott The Daily Telegraph.

author: John Mullen
title: Will the French have a fascist president next May? Questions and answers about the far right in France today
content:
The upcoming French presidential election next May carries weight far beyond France’s borders.

A victory for fascist candidate Marine Le Pen — in a major world economy — would embolden far-right movements globally while dealing a terrible blow to French workers, particularly women, LGBT+ people and Muslims.

Conversely, a win for the radical left candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon, of the France Insoumise (France in Revolt, FI)[1] would offer an important boost to anti-capitalists everywhere.

This election will be anything but business as usual. A recent poll revealed that 71% of voters want the new president to bring about “real social and political change”.[2]

This Q and A aims to explain the key dynamics at work, as well as the strengths and weaknesses of antifascist activity in France today.

Will the French have a fascist president next May?

Nobody can know the answer to this question right now, but the danger is very real. Far-right candidate Marine Le Pen of the Rassemblement National (National Rally, RN) is the favourite in the polls, with around 33% of voting intentions for the first round.[3] No other candidate polls above 20%.

Le Pen has particularly gained ground in recent years among women voters[4] and public sector workers, traditionally populations where the left is strong.

A quarter of public sector workers who say they feel close to a political party cite RN a

author: Suzanne James
title: NT Country Liberal Party passes ‘obstructive’ VAD law
content:
After a relentless 30-year grassroots campaign, including the 2022 overturning of Kevin Andrews 1997 Commonwealth veto, assisted dying rights have finally been restored to the Northern Territory with the Rights of the Terminally Ill Act 2026 passing on August 27.

But while voluntary assisted dying (VAD) will now be legal Australia-wide, advocates remain concerned about the inclusion of two discredited and obstructive “safeguards”, which makes the lawl far less accessible than its 1995 namesake.

The new VAD law was one of the most anticipated conscience votes in the Northern Territory. Reserved for contentious social or bioethical matters that divide public and parliamentary opinion across party lines, the premise of a conscience vote rests on three pillars: Suspension of party discipline; individual judgement on matters of personal morality or individual conscience; and leadership permission, where the leader and senior members of the party officially grant MPs permission.

NT Attorney General Marie-Clare Boothby first confirmed on January 2 that the Country Liberal Party (CLP) would introduce a VAD bill in “mid-2026” and that she would be “voting in favour”.

The NT Chief Minister Lia Finocchiaro told a community forum in June that it was on the parliamentary agenda, stating again it would be a free vote for all Members of the Legislative Assembly (MLAs). She then announced

author: Cameron Mitchell
title: ‘No Bystanders’ concert highlights violence against women, raises funds for charities
content:
Caitlin Davies with the support of Australian Femicide Watch, Socialist Alliance, Violent Butterfly Records and other activist groups organised a fundraising concert on September 5 to highlight and educate people about violence against women.

The mixed-bill hardcore concert, titled No Bystanders, heard from 14 local bands, which volunteered to allow ticket proceeds to go to relevant charities.

The all-ages concert included face painting for children and adults, provided by Rhee Brown, and merchandise stalls which lined the Royal Park Hall venue, between two stages.

Each band, hosting several mosh pits, drew an impressive crowd. The energy of the punk/metal music matched the anger felt towards the injustice women face.

The stories of women who have become victim to femicide were highlighted. The wall was filled with faces of women who had been killed by men from 2024 to 2026. The memorial allowed participants to write letters to be read by speakers affected by domestic violence.

Two women, in particular, were the focus of photo collages: Ebony Lee and Ali Lauren. Lee, a close friend of Davies, had her life taken earlier this year. Lauren, a local, was murdered last year by a conspiracy theory podcaster.

Davies said a fundraiser after Lee’s death had raised $46,000 for victims of male violence, and was one of the main inspirations behind No Bystanders.

author: Pip Hinman
title: Socialist Alliance NSW calls for moratorium on AI mega data centres
content:
Socialist Alliance NSW said it wholeheartedly supports community calls for a moratorium on the construction of artificial intelligence mega data centres.

“The expansion of mega data centres in Australia is mostly unregulated. Many of the industrial sites slated for mega data centres are right next to residential areas,” Isaac Nellist who is standing for Socialist Alliance in Balmain, told Green Left.

There are 47 artificial intelligence (AI) mega data centres being planned in NSW, including 20 State Significant Developments and 15 key projects.

“These mega data centres mostly use excessive water and energy and are likely to destabilise local supplies. We note that the Victorian government has moved to quell legitimate community anxiety about the rapid construction of these mega data centres.

“It says it will ‘set the rules’, including that they must use their own renewable energy supply and storage, meet connection costs and network upgrades and use recycled or non-drinking water for cooling.

“But another key issue is where these constructions are sited: Victorian Labor has promised a ‘buffer’ between homes and data centres — but of only 150 metres. This will not allay community concerns about noise and other pollution.”

Socialist Alliance also shares community concerns about what these centres are being used for.

“The new mega AI data centres are predominantly used to s

author: Jackie Kriz
title: Socialist Alliance: Ben Carroll’s CFMEU royal commission spends big money on a ‘farce’
content:
Tim Gooden and Sue Bull, who are members of the Construction Forestry Mining Employees Union in Victoria, described the royal commission into the union set up by Premier Ben Carroll as a “farce”.

Together with Maritime Union of Australia member Ross Smith, they are standing for Socialist Alliance for the Western Victoria Region in the November 28 election.

After the first public hearing day of the Royal Commission into the Integrity of Major Public and Civil Infrastructure Construction Projects in Victoria on September 23 — which lasted a whole hour and fifty minutes — they said it “smacks of a show trial”. It broke for a long lunch and then adjourned. It now won’t reconvene for some time.

As Gooden, a former union official, shop steward and construction worker commented to Green Left: “Can you imagine the outcry if construction workers turned up at 10am for work, nicked off to the pub at lunchtime and then disappeared for several weeks? Meanwhile, according to the establishment media, CFMEU members are supposedly all on the take, as well as being ‘thugs’.”

Bull, a health and safety trainer in the construction industry for many years, told GL: “If yesterday’s hearing is any indication, this commission will spend $50 million over 12 months to unearth more rumour and innuendo. “Chris Young KC, Council assisting the commission, has already claimed that ex-CFMEU officials force

author: Susan Price
title: Campaign to name and shame companies fuelling Indonesia’s wildfire crisis
content:
An escalating wildfire crisis in Indonesia since July has covered much of Southeast Asia in a protracted and hazardous smoke haze.

Greenpeace Malaysia and Himpunan Advocacy Rakyat Malaysia (HARAM) held a peaceful protest outside the Indonesian embassy in Malaysia’s capital, Kuala Lumpur, on September 4, in solidarity with all communities affected by the cross-border haze and the loss of wildlife, suffered most severely in Indonesia.

The protesters did not blame Indonesians for the crisis but, instead called for the corporate interests that are complicit in the crisis — including Malaysian companies — to be named and shamed.

"While corporate executives sit comfortably in their air-conditioned offices earning millions of dollars in profit, it is the common citizens, workers, students and even the children of Malaysia and Indonesia who are breathing in and dying from the haze. Schools are closing down, and our basic human right to breathe is being taken away from us. Clean air doesn’t have a passport, nor does environmental devastation. We stand firmly in solidarity with the communities in Indonesia who are affected by these fires,” HARAM chairman Brendon Gan said in a statement.

“Our action called on the government of Indonesia to formally disclose concession maps, hotspot and fire investigation data, and other evidence identifying Malaysian-linked companies associated with f

author: Tim Gooden
title: AMWU organiser says workers gain from four-day work week
content:
Many workers here are now enjoying a four-day working week and a longer week-end, every week, due to a campaign by the Australian Manufacturing Workers Union.

Tony Hynds, an industrial organiser for the Australian Manufacturing Workers Union (AMWU), told Green Left that workers were wary of the four-day week idea.

“At first workers were very sceptical about the idea,” Hynds said. “At my first members’ meeting of a few hundred people, I was heckled and accused of selling out the rostered day off (RDO) ... But, after a while the idea caught on.

“With no loss of pay or conditions, workers would actually gain and every weekend was a long weekend. That was five years ago; now everyone loves it and would not go back to the RDO system.”

He said the four day work week essentially squashes the 38-hour, five-day week into four days. That means working four time 9.5-hour days, plus the traditional half-hour unpaid lunch break.

There are a couple of versions being adopted right now.

Some companies and groups of members have opted for every Monday off, with overtime if they do work on the Monday.

The other option is that the workplace is split into two groups, with one taking Fridays off and the other taking Mondays off, but the workplace is open five days a week.

Workers at the Geelong Refinery opted for the first version, where everyone works from Tuesday to Friday as their normal

author: Kerry Smith
title: Protest demands NSW Police stop harassing LGBTIQ people
content:
A snap action called to protest NSW Police raids on gay bars in Oxford Street, Darlinghurst, drew 100 people to Taylor Square. 

Kerry Smith

 reports.

author: Pip Hinman
title: We need to stand up against genocide
content:
Cathy Eatock gave the following speech to the International Day of Peace rally on September 20 on Gadigal Country, organised by Sydney Anti-AUKUS Coalition and Stop the War on Palestine.

AUKUS ties us irrevocably to the United States war machine.

Australia has previously blindly followed the US into the war on terror which led to the deaths of an estimated 4.7 million people in Iraq, Syria and Libya.

Now the Anthony Albanese government has, astoundingly, followed Scott Morrison into AUKUS, without question or public discussion. The obscene cost of $368 billion over 30 years means hospitals, aged care homes, housing, education, the National Disability Support Scheme, dental and mental health services, and Aboriginal communities won’t receive the funding we need.

With each submarine having its own nuclear reactor, its radioactive waste will need to be stored here.

But Aboriginal people have repeatedly rejected even low-grade medical uranium waste being stored on their lands. The Aboriginal communities of Maralinga, Emu plain and Montebello Islands have already borne the brunt of nuclear testing.

Pacific peoples in the Marshall Islands, Christmas Island, French Polynesia and Kiribati have endured 315 nuclear weapons tests. It is the Pacific and Aboriginal communities that continues to suffer that legacy.

As well as the initial deaths, blindness, radiation sickness, there ar

author: Sue Bolton
title: Labor must stop helping One Nation scapegoat migrants
content:
Home affairs and immigration minister Tony Burke’s speech to the National Press Club (NPC) on September 17 was a boost to Pauline Hanson’s One Nation and its Trumpite politics of hate, racism and division.

Burke’s speech, delayed for a month, was always framed as Labor’s “new” plan to get tougher on immigration.

It was a blatant concession to One Nation’s billionaire-funded campaign to scapegoat recent and non-European migrants for the housing and cost-of-living crisis, despite them being a result of the establishment parties’ neoliberal policies since the 1980s.

This bipartisan approach is responsible for making housing totally unaffordable for a new generation of workers. It has reduced real wages and eroded basic social rights, including the right to public health, education, transport and welfare.

Migrant workers are not the cause of these problems. However, with the backing of Gina Rinehart, Australia’s wealthiest billionaire, Hanson has whipped up a panic about “mass migration”; it is her way way of shifting the blame from the billionaire class to the most vulnerable sections of the working class.

Burke said that One Nation’s claims about “mass migration” were “absurd” and “not something we're dealing with in Australia”. But he went on to outline measures to cut net overseas migration from 290,000 to 225,000, in 2027-28, and make life harder for migrant workers and i

author: Isaac Nellist, Ben Radford
title: On The Streets: Arts workers on strike and students rally against sexual violence
content:
On The Streets is a podcast by Green Left giving you bite-sized updates about the protest movements and grassroots campaigns across the country.

On this episode, we discuss Ecosocialism 2026, arts workers on strike in Naarm/Melbourne and the student rally against sexual violence.

Find more upcoming events here.

author: Susan Price
title: ‘Ecological crisis creates a challenge and an opportunity for the left’
content:
Ayesha Ahmad, a Pakistani socialist-feminist activist, researcher, educator, and labour rights practitioner with the Haqooq-e-Khalq Party, was one of the guest speakers at the Ecosocialism 2026 conference in Magan-djin/Brisbane, September 11–13. She spoke to Green Left’s Peter Boyle about the impact of the mounting global ecological crisis on politics in Pakistan.

The catastrophic flash floods in Nepal as a result of global warming and the melting of the Himalayan glaciers were a warning to the world, but does it have a special significance for Pakistan, which also borders the Himalayas?

The catastrophic flash floods in Nepal are a profound warning for Pakistan. For years, Pakistan has been among the countries most exposed to the climate crisis in South Asia, and we have already witnessed what a warming Himalaya can do — from the catastrophic 2022 floods, to increasingly frequent glacial lake outburst floods in Gilgit-Baltistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. The Nepal disaster tells us that we may be entering an even more dangerous phase of the Himalayan climate crisis.

But for me, there is a much deeper question here. South Asia shares a history. We share the history of colonial extraction, of loot and plunder, of resources being taken from our lands to build wealth elsewhere. Political decolonisation did not necessarily mean economic decolonisation. The geography of extraction ha

author: Susan Price
title: Timor-Leste’s struggle for freedom and the politics of refugee protection
content:
The Good Sea: The Journey of the ‘Tasi Diak’ and the Politics of Refugee Protection in Australia By Vannessa Hearman Melbourne University Press (2026) 256pp. $36.99

A small boat set out from occupied East Timor (Timor-Leste), bound for Darwin on May 24, 1995. On board were 17 activists who had been campaigning against the Indonesian occupation of their homeland, as well as a six-month-old baby.

Some of the passengers had participated in protests that had been violently repressed by the Indonesian army. Some had given support to the guerrilla resistance fighters in the mountains. Now, they wanted to take the case for Timor-Leste’s independence to the people of Australia and the world.

The Good Sea: The Journey of the ‘Tasi Diak’ and the Politics of Refugee Protection in Australia tells the story of their voyage and their experiences before and after.

Author Vannessa Hearman, born in Indonesia and based at Curtin University in Western Australia, is a historian of Southeast Asia, specialising in political violence, human rights and historical memory in Indonesia and Timor-Leste.

The book covers a range of political issues, including Indonesian invasion and occupation; the Australian government’s decades of support for the occupation and its eventual change of policy; Australia’s treatment of refugees; and the development of the movements in solidarity with Timor-Leste and in

author: Isaac Nellist
title: Students walk out of class again to protest Hanson’s racism and bigotry
content:
Thousands of high school and university students again walked out of class a second time to protest Pauline Hanson’s racism and bigotry on September 17. Rallies were held in 18 cities and towns across the country.

Students highlighted Hanson’s racist comments towards First Nations people and immigrants, her anti-LGBTIQ stance, her claim that domestic violence is a “two-way street” and her denial of the climate crisis.

Many pointed out that Hanson’s claim to be representing “ordinary Australians” is shown to be a lie because she is backed by Gina Rinehart, Australia’s richest person, and has consistently voted against pay rises and improved workers’ rights.

Students at the rally in Gadigal Country/Sydney told Green Left they did not support the vision for the country that Hanson is putting forward. “We’re the next generation of voters and we don’t want to see people like Pauline Hanson and One Nation who spread bigotry and hate in power,” one student said.

A year-12 student told Green Left he attended the protest to oppose Hanson’s racist rhetoric, and its adoption by Labor and the Coalition. “I’m here to stand in solidarity with women, immigrants, Palestinians, Indigenous people and queer people.”

Another student said they want politicians who are “for the people and not for billionaires”. “My mum is a person of colour and we don’t want someone who’s going to be racist.”

author: Pip Hinman
title: Socialist Alliance trade unionists to contest Western Victoria Region
content:
Socialist Alliance in Victoria has announced candidates for the Legislative Council in the Western Victoria Region at the November 28 elections.

The party is running on the campaign theme of “Fighting for people, not the billionaires”.

Tim Gooden, Sue Bull and Ross Smith are active trade unionists from the construction and maritime industries, and think progressive working class people need to be heard.

Gooden, a former Secretary of Geelong Trades Hall and a Palestine justice campaigner, told Green Left: “We are putting forward positive solutions for workers rather than the hate which is being put out by the big end of town. Blaming migrants and refugees for cost-of-living rises is about scapegoating people who have nothing. Meanwhile, the billionaires rake in profits.”

Bull, a teacher trainer in schools and the construction industry for many years told GL: “State and federal governments can always find money to subsidise their big business mates, but when it comes to funding housing, health or education, the coffers are bare. We need to build a movement that fights for us and our needs.”

author: Pip Hinman
title: Ecosocialism 2026 forges unity and builds struggles
content:
“The big people behind capitalism are quite aware that they are planning the end of the world as we know it”, Sabrina Fernandes, a political economist and ecosocialist activist from Brazil, told the Ecosocialism 2026 conference in Magan-djin/Brisbane, September 11–13.

“They don’t have a problem with the world ending as we know it — as long as they can keep making profits,” Fernandes said.

“They do have a problem with a society that they might not be able to control when things get really hard, as we are coming to this stage of ecocide and global catastrophe. They are fighting over the spoils of war and climate change.”

Places that would not normally be considered part of the grab are becoming so, Fernandes said. The oceans “are a new terra nullius for them” — for ocean floor mining.

There should be an international agreement for this, but US President Donald Trump does not care and has begun issuing his own licences, she added.

Helen Yaffe, author, activist and Professor of Latin American Political Economy, University of Glasgow, told the conference that socialist Cuba, one of the key targets of Trump’s new colonialism, is facing multiple and mounting challenges as the US blockade intensifies.

The response that she has witnessed, in a recent visit to Cuba, was: “We shall not submit!”

author: Susan Price
title: ‘The Return’ uses magical realism to confront Israel’s genocide
content:
Jordan Shukri AK Armaou-Massoud

The Return Written and directed by Ala’a Al Qaisi Touring Sydney, Melbourne and regional Victoria Visit thereturnproject.com.au for details

Green Left’s Jordan Shukri AK Armaou-Massoud caught up with award-winning Palestinian writer director Ala’a Al Qaisi about her play, The Return, which has been touring Sydney, Melbourne and regional Victoria since September 1.

“As war tears through Gaza, a father waits for the clouds to bring his daughters home.”

So reads the synopsis for The Return, a powerfully surreal stage play written and directed by award-winning Palestinian writer director Ala’a Al Qaisi.

Al Qaisi told Green Left her idea for the play started early into Israel’s genocidal war on the Palestinians, when she saw a video of a father from Gaza whose name is Marwan Abu Samra.

Marwan was in a hospital next to his daughter Nagham — a famous karate champion who represented Palestine whenever she could leave Gaza to travel. Nagham’s leg had been amputated and she was in a coma — the result of an Israeli airstrike.

“[Marwan] already lost Rozan, his other daughter, in the same strike, and he was cleaving to the wall to help him get Nagham out of Gaza to get treatment because, at the time, they didn’t even have any antibiotics to save her,” Al Qaisi said.

author: Pip Hinman
title: Big data and the AUKUS war machine
content:
The world’s greatest remilitarisation since the World War II is underway, driven by the imperatives of the flailing United States empire.

The AUKUS war pact places us at the centre of this drive towards war. How should we imagine Australia’s role in the world?

Australia is not just a settler-colonial state; it is a sub-imperial power that has transferred subordination from its one-time colonial ruler, Britain, to the US, its new imperial master.

It is now acting to preserve the military and economic interests of its master state. This is encapsulated in the AUKUS war pact, which, despite no public debate, commits the country to eight nuclear-powered submarines, high-tech weapons development and sharing and the subsequent invasion of US personnel and weaponry in the event of our “interoperability” in a contrived future conflict with China.

Through AUKUS, Australia acts as a mechanism for US force projection into the Pacific, to rattle the sabre against China.

AUKUS makes Australia the first non-nuclear-weapons state to use a loophole in the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons for naval propulsion with weapons-grade uranium.

That sets a proliferation precedent.

author: Pip Hinman
title: Greens divided over koala park carbon credit scam
content:
Federal Labor has maintained its unwavering support for the fossil fuel industry against persistent community demands for genuine climate action by voting down a disallowance motion that would have blocked the so-called Improved Native Forest Management (INFM) system.

Controversially, seven of 10 Australian Greens Senators voted with Labor on September 10. But Greens Senators Nick McKim, Jordon Steele-John and Vanessa Bleyer supported the motion, although not because they agreed with the Nationals-One Nation movers.

The WA Greens MPs said that they “strongly opposed” the INFM method and were “disappointed” that colleagues voted with Labor, “thereby allowing the INFM method to remain in place”. They said the INFM system could generate 1.5 million carbon credits.

Supporters of the Labor-Green deal say it will save koalas and forest habitat.

Greens leader Larissa Waters said: “These improvements will help deliver the Great Koala National Park (GKNP) in NSW, protecting 176,000 hectares of native forest and safeguarding habitat for around 12,000 koalas and more than 100 other threatened species”.

However, it also means that saving forests and koalas relies on creating new carbon credits in an already dodgy carbon trading market.

author: Isaac Nellist
title: Activists face charges in Singapore
content:
Anti-death penalty activists Jolovan Wham and Elijah Tay faced court on September 7 and 9, charged with 19 offences under Singapore’s Public Order Act and Penal Code.

Tay, who is also a campaigner in solidarity with Palestinians against Israel’s genocidal war in Gaza, participated in the Ecosocialism 2024 conference in Boorloo/Perth.

Tay is being charged with: participating in candlelight vigils for death row inmates; participating in a photo outside the state court where people had their fists raised and were all wearing “not in my name” t-shirts in solidarity with people sentenced to death; organising a shoe memorial for children martyred in Gaza outside an Israeli-linked research building at Singapore’s national university; participating in a walk to the Ministry of Home Affairs to deliver feedback about a proposed government law that would be detrimental to free speech; chanting “from the river to the sea, Palestine will be free” at a private indoor assembly livestreamed on social media; and for not answering a public servant (likely a police officer) during questioning.

Wham, who is an anti-death penalty activist, is also being charged with participating in a candlelight vigil for death row inmates; organising an assembly outside the state courts; and not answering a public servant during questioning, among other charges.

author: Susan Price
title: ‘We can all have a good life and live within planetary boundaries’
content:
See Yong Feng was one of the guest speakers at the Ecosocialism 2026 conference in Magan-djin/Brisbane on September 11–13. He explained in his presentation, “Degrowth and Ecosocialism”, how it would be possible for all people — in the Global South and Global North — to have a good life without crossing planetary boundaries.

See previously worked as an architect and returned to Singapore last year after completing a Masters in political ecology, environmental justice and degrowth at the Autonomous University of Barcelona. He currently works in book publishing and organises with Singapore Climate Rally as well as the independent media network NIMBUS.

During the conference, See spoke with Green Left’s Peter Boyle about degrowth and how humanity can live within planetary boundaries.

You studied under Professor Jason Hickel at the Autonomous University of Barcelona. He has been at the cutting edge of debates and discussions around ecosocialism and degrowth. What do you think are the most important areas of research that Hickel and his team have covered in the past couple of years?

Research has been done to quantify and prove to conventional economists — and other people who need to see the facts — the extent of the extraction and exploitation that’s going on.

author: Pip Hinman
title: Join International Day of Peace protests to scrap AUKUS, stop war on Gaza
content:
Anti-war and solidarity groups are protesting across the country, September 12–21, to demand an end to the war alliance with the United States and for AUKUS to be scrapped.

September 15 also marks the fifth anniversary of the Coalition government signing the AUKUS Pillar I and II pact with the US and Britain. Labor adopted AUKUS as its own and has refused to support a parliamentary inquiry.

New publicly released data shows that the US military and weapons corporations control, or have unimpeded access, to more than 100 military facilities across Australia. More than half of the military facilities in this country are controlled, or used extensively, by the US military, in preparation for a major war.

AUKUS is supposedly costing upwards of $368 billion over the next 30 years. That means some $35 million a day is being siphoned away from health, education, affordable housing and many urgent social needs to fund wars of aggression and weapons corporations.

As the US and Israel make the world a more dangerous place, Labor continues to give its support to both, including by sending weapons parts to Israel for its F-35 fighter jet parts.

Australia also supplies intelligence through the Pine Gap spy base in central Australia, which can be used by Israel to pinpoint targets.
